During his brief visit this time, Emma had hardly seen him, though enough to get their first meeting over with and to feel that the wounded pride and self-importance now colouring his manner did nothing to improve him. Indeed, she was beginning to wonder how she had ever found him agreeable at all. Seeing him was so closely bound up with painful feelings that, apart from its moral value as a penance, a lesson, an opportunity for salutary humiliation, she would have been grateful for a promise never to encounter him again. She wished him every happiness; but his presence hurt her, and she would take greatest satisfaction in his prosperity twenty miles away.

The discomfort of his continuing to live in Highbury, however, would certainly diminish with his marriage. It would spare them many unnecessary anxieties and ease many awkward situations. A Mrs. Elton would provide an explanation for any change in their dealings; their former closeness could fade without attracting comment. They could almost begin their polite acquaintance afresh.

Emma gave very little thought to the woman herself. No doubt she was good enough for Mr. Elton, accomplished enough for Highbury, and handsome enough—probably to seem plain beside Harriet. As for her family connections, Emma felt entirely at ease. She was convinced that, despite his much-proclaimed claims and his contempt for Harriet, he had gained nothing there. On that point, the truth seemed discoverable. What sort of woman she was must remain uncertain, but who she was could be established; and apart from the ten thousand pounds, nothing suggested that she was Harriet’s superior. She brought no distinguished name, noble ancestry, or important alliances. Miss Hawkins was the younger of two daughters of a Bristol—merchant, of course, one must call him. But since the entire proceeds of his business career seemed so modest, it was hardly unjust to suppose that his particular trade had been modest in standing too. She had generally spent part of each winter in Bath, but Bristol was her home, the very centre of Bristol. Although both her parents had died some years before, an uncle remained, employed in the law. No more precisely respectable description was ventured than that he worked in the law; and the daughter had lived with him. Emma imagined him doing the drudgery for some attorney, too dull to advance. All the splendour of the connection seemed to rest on the elder sister, who had married extremely well: a gentleman with a very substantial business near Bristol, who kept two carriages! That was the grand conclusion of the account; that was Miss Hawkins’s crowning distinction.

You must adopt a little of my philosophy. Think about the past only when remembering it brings you pleasure.”

“I cannot credit you with that sort of philosophy. When you look back, you must find so little to blame yourself for that your satisfaction comes from something much better than philosophy: not knowing what regret is. With me, things are different. Painful memories force their way in, and I cannot, and should not, drive them away. All my life I have behaved selfishly, though my principles were better than my actions. As a child, I learned what was right, but no one taught me to control my temper. I was given sound principles, then allowed to practise them with pride and conceit. Unfortunately, as an only son—and for many years an only child—I was spoiled by my parents. They were good people themselves, and my father especially was kind and generous. Yet they allowed, encouraged, almost taught me to be selfish and domineering, to care for nobody outside my family, and to look down on everyone else. At least, they taught me to want to believe that others had less sense and less worth than I did. That was how I lived from eight until twenty-eight, and I might still be the same without you, my dearest, most lovely Elizabeth! How much I owe you! You taught me a lesson that was painful at first, but did me immense good. You humbled me as I deserved. When I approached you, I had no doubt that you would welcome me. You showed me how little all my supposed advantages could do to win a woman worth winning.”

“Had you really convinced yourself that I would?”

“Yes, I had. What must you think of my vanity? I believed you wanted and expected me to propose.”

“My behaviour must have been misleading, but I assure you it was unintentional. I never meant to deceive you, though my high spirits may often have led me astray. How you must have hated me after that evening!”

“Hated you! Perhaps I was angry at first, but I soon began to direct my anger where it belonged.”

“I am almost afraid to ask what you thought when we met at Pemberley. Did you blame me for coming?”

“Certainly not. I was simply surprised.”

“You cannot have been more surprised than I was when you acknowledged me. My conscience told me I deserved no special kindness, and I admit I did not expect more than I deserved.”

“My aim then,” Darcy replied, “was to show you every possible courtesy, so that you would see I was not petty enough to hold the past against you. I hoped to earn your forgiveness and improve your opinion of me by showing that I had listened to your criticism.

It was the last of Lady Windermere’s receptions before Easter, and Bentinck House was more thronged than ever. Six Cabinet Ministers had arrived from the Speaker’s Levée, wearing their stars and ribands; every pretty woman had put on her finest gown; and at the far end of the picture-gallery stood Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe, a large lady of Tartar appearance, with minute black eyes and magnificent emeralds, speaking execrable French at the utmost pitch of her voice and laughing extravagantly at whatever anyone told her. The gathering was certainly a remarkable mixture. Splendid peeresses conversed pleasantly with fierce Radicals, fashionable preachers rubbed coat-tails with distinguished unbelievers, and a whole flock of bishops pursued a portly prima-donna through successive rooms. Several Royal Academicians stood upon the stairs in the disguise of artists, while rumour had it that at one moment the supper-room was positively packed with geniuses. Altogether, it was among Lady Windermere’s greatest evenings, and the Princess remained until almost half-past eleven.

Once she had departed, Lady Windermere went back to the picture-gallery, where a famous political economist was gravely expounding the scientific theory of music to an affronted Hungarian virtuoso, and entered into conversation with the Duchess of Paisley. She was astonishingly lovely, with her stately ivory throat, her great forget-me-not-blue eyes, and the thick golden coils of her hair. Pure gold they were—not the pallid straw shade that now lays claim to that gracious name, but gold of the kind threaded through sunlight or concealed in curious amber. About her face they formed something of a saint’s frame, accompanied by a considerable share of a sinner’s charm. Psychologically, she offered a singular study. She had learnt early the essential truth that an indiscretion bears the closest resemblance to innocence; and a succession of daring adventures, half perfectly harmless, had won her every privilege accorded to a personality. Her husband she had changed more than once—Debrett, indeed, assigns her three marriages—but her lover had always remained the same, and society had long since abandoned scandalous talk about her. She was forty now, without children, and possessed that excessive appetite for pleasure which is the secret of continued youth.

All at once she glanced eagerly about the room and asked in her clear contralto, ‘Where has my cheiromantist gone?’

‘Your what, Gladys?’ cried the Duchess, starting despite herself.

‘My cheiromantist, Duchess. Just now I cannot exist without him.’

‘My dear Gladys, you are invariably so original,’ the Duchess murmured, attempting to recollect precisely what a cheiromantist was, and trusting that it did not mean a cheiropodist.

‘He visits me to examine my hand regularly twice each week,’ Lady Windermere went on, ‘and has the most interesting things to say about it.’
